answer.rationale: Rolling back the security-patched release is ruled out by compliance (memory_b1's rollback lesson doesn't apply to a release compliance forbids reverting). Settlement peak rules out read-replica shunting as a write-path lever (the b5 read-replica trick targets dashboard/report reads, not write p99). Regional failover (b2) shifts traffic but doesn't reduce write load and risks abandoning in-flight settlements at peak. Adding capacity is the slowest of the options and the surge profile (heavy writes, climbing p99) suggests backpressure/contention rather than pure headroom. The b4 memory is the direct precedent: a payments-dependency circuit breaker contained a partner-side failure by failing fast and preserving the rest of checkout. At 5x p99 with writes heavy, the most likely contributor is a downstream dependency stalling under load and queuing the write path; a targeted circuit breaker on the suspect dependency confines the blast radius, preserves customer writes on the healthy path, and—unlike rollback, failover, or capacity—does not conflict with the compliance-mandated security patch. b1 is verified because it closes the door on rollback definitively; b4 is verified to confirm the breaker pattern and blast-radius behavior observed in this exact environment. One intervention only, per the budget.
